sections.heading: Progressive Container Deserialization and Soft Limits
sections.summary: Clients are re-adding hard limits at the SSZ layer for progressive containers; Justin will discuss adding optional limit support to the SSZ spec library with Eitan.
sections.body:
- Enrico (Teku) observed that the community is moving back toward having hard limits enforced at the SSZ deserialization layer, which partially negates the benefit of progressive containers that were designed to be unbounded.
  - The advantage that remains: changing limits in a future fork will not break provers or require large SSZ layout changes, because generalized indices stay constant.
- Teku finds the current spec test situation awkward: state transition tests include inputs with list lengths exceeding the soft limit, but Teku's SSZ library rejects them at deserialization before the state transition function even runs.
  - Justin suggested a general rule: if SSZ deserialization fails and the test's expected post-state is null, treat the test as a success.
  - Enrico acknowledged this could work but called it "not ideal" because it masks potential unrelated deserialization bugs.
- Lodestar (Nico) already updated its test harness to handle these invalid-limit tests; the tests fail as expected during deserialization, and it was not a lot of changes.
- Prysm has [a PR open](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/prysm/pull/17412) to add these limits at unmarshalling. Potuz expressed concern that hard-coding limits in the unmarshalling layer is a consensus bug waiting to happen if limits change in a future fork and someone forgets to update the hard-coded values.
- Enrico raised that the `deposit_requests` field in the Gloas BeaconBlock currently has no soft limit defined and should be set to zero, since legacy deposits are not expected in Gloas.
  - Nico confirmed Lodestar already cannot deserialize a Gloas block with non-zero legacy deposits.
  - Enrico volunteered to open a PR for adding the zero limit on the deposit field.
- Agreement that all fields except execution requests and transactions should have soft limits enforced at SSZ deserialization; execution requests and transactions remain bounded only by the gas limit and the 10 MB gossip limit.
- Justin will discuss with Eitan and the SSZ specs library maintainer (Tama C) about introducing optional limits in the progressive list Python library so specs and clients can handle limits consistently.
- Nico raised that even with these limits, deposit_requests remain effectively unbounded (only limited by gas limit), meaning a DoS attack could still exploit the 10 MB gossip limit.
  - Grandine (Saulius) noted that the 10 MB limit has historically been interpreted differently across clients (some measure compressed, some uncompressed, some include metadata).
  - Pawan (Lighthouse) clarified that the limit was previously unified to mean maximum uncompressed payload size, and clients fixed their implementations at that time.
  - The 10 MB limit is defined in the [P2P spec](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/blob/f21dac06e99743b1e98bb80297897b96520c942b/specs/phase0/p2p-interface.md?plain=1#L492-L512) as the maximum allowed size of uncompressed payload in gossipsub messages and RPC chunks.

sections.heading: Equivocations in Fork Choice
sections.summary: Prysm counts invalid (signature-only) equivocations for proposer boost decisions; other clients only count valid ones per spec — Potuz will open a PR to align the spec.
sections.body:
- Potuz explained that fork choice only becomes aware of blocks after they pass full validation (via `on_block`), but equivocation detection and proposer boost decisions must happen earlier, at gossip time.
  - Equivocating blocks are never imported into fork choice over gossip — only via RPC when syncing a branch that contains an equivocation.
  - The `should_apply_proposer_boost` and `is_proposer_equivocation` functions are the relevant checks ([spec links shared](https://ethereum.github.io/spec-viewer/#consensus/nightly/functions-should_apply_proposer_boost-gloas)).
- Prysm's approach: as soon as a valid signature is seen on a second block from the same proposer/slot, fork choice is signaled about the equivocation regardless of whether the block itself is fully valid. Prysm also tracks timeliness and ordering of equivocations.
- Other clients (following the Python spec literally) only count equivocations from blocks that pass full validation, which Potuz considers incorrect behavior.
- Potuz argued that fork choice and P2P behaviors — things not part of the core state transition function — are over-specified in the Python executable spec, causing clients to implement the letter rather than the intent.
- Enrico (Teku) acknowledged Teku does not currently have equivocation detection signaled from gossip into fork choice, and would need to add it.
- Nico (Lodestar) asked whether Prysm validates signatures on more than the first two observed proposals from the same slot, raising a DoS concern: a proposer could craft thousands of differently-signed blocks.
  - Potuz confirmed Prysm validates the signature on every incoming equivocating block and acknowledged this could be a DoS vector, since libp2p message IDs would differ for each block.
  - Potuz offered to add code to stop verifying after the third block.
- Potuz agreed to open a PR to update the spec, with Justin offering to help with test changes. Potuz noted his preference would be to under-specify fork choice behavior rather than encode it in executable Python.

sections.heading: Deprecating mplex
sections.summary: All clients support deprecating mplex by Gloas mainnet; Teku's QUIC implementation needs refinement but is actively being worked on and is not a blocker.
sections.body:
- Justin raised the topic of deprecating mplex ([consensus-specs PR #3866](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/3866)).
- Potuz asked if anyone opposes deprecation; no one objected.
  - Potuz also mentioned wanting to get rid of yamux eventually.
- Lighthouse ([PR #9522](https://github.com/sigp/lighthouse/pull/9522)) has already merged the change to drop mplex, as previously arranged. jxs (Lighthouse) expressed frustration that this has been dragging for years and that the Rust mplex implementation is unmaintained, calling it a potential attack vector.
- Enrico (Teku) reported that Teku's QUIC implementation is working in production but still has issues to fix (including memory leaks). A default-configured Teku node currently gets ~70-75% QUIC connections and ~20% TCP.
  - Teku has yamux support via jvm-libp2p but it is not production-ready.
  - Enrico said he does not see a blocker to deprecating mplex by Gloas mainnet, but needs additional refinement time.
  - Enrico has personally disabled TCP on his own node.
- Pawan (Lighthouse) noted that last time the blocker was Teku lacking QUIC/yamux, which now appears resolved.
- No final decision on whether to deprecate in-fork or out-of-fork; Enrico indicated Gloas mainnet timing is reasonable.
